title: Loop back: the tricky inputs
idea: LOOP (review). Revisit the edge-case habit (empty, zero, one item, boundary) from Unit 80-81 across different patterns.

exercises.prompt: Review: which input is the tricky EDGE case for averaging a list?
options: An empty list — dividing by zero items breaks
A list of three normal numbers
Any list with more than one item
exercises.explanation: An empty list means count 0, and dividing by 0 crashes. Always guard the empty case before an average.

exercises.prompt: Review: a 'track the biggest' helper seeds best = items[0]. Which input breaks that very line?
options: An empty list — there is no items[0]
exercises.explanation: items[0] needs at least one item. On an empty list it crashes — the empty edge case strikes again.

exercises.prompt: Review: a sum helper handles an empty list fine, returning 0.
exercises.explanation: Yes. total starts at 0 and the loop just doesn't run, so empty gives 0. Not every pattern needs an empty guard — summing is safe.

exercises.prompt: Review: which pattern NEEDS an empty guard to avoid a crash?
exercises.explanation: Dividing by the count breaks at count 0. Sum and count handle empty naturally (they return 0); the divide needs the guard.

exercises.prompt: Review (boundary): a pass is 'at least 50'. A score of exactly 50 should...
exercises.explanation: 'At least 50' includes 50, so >= 50. Testing a value exactly on the boundary catches < vs <= bugs.

exercises.prompt: Review: match each task to the edge case worth testing first.
exercises.explanation: Each pattern has a boundary input that stresses it. Listing them while planning stops bugs before they happen.

exercises.prompt: Review: a single-item list [7]. The biggest is...
options: 7 — the only item is the biggest
exercises.explanation: With one item, it is trivially the biggest. A correct track-the-biggest helper handles the single-item edge fine.

exercises.prompt: Review: enumerating edge cases DURING planning is better than waiting for a crash.
exercises.explanation: Yes — the whole edge-case habit. Think of empty, zero, one, and boundary inputs up front so the helper handles them on purpose.

exercises.prompt: Review: why do edge-case bugs survive casual testing?
options: Everyday inputs are far from the edges, so the one bad case rarely appears
They only happen in huge programs
exercises.explanation: The bug bites only at the edge. Unless you deliberately test empty/zero/one/boundary, normal inputs look fine and hide it.

options: List the edge cases (empty, zero, one, boundary) per pattern and guard the ones that would crash or lie
Every pattern needs an empty guard
exercises.explanation: Enumerating edges is prevention. Some patterns need a guard (average), some don't (sum). Knowing which is the skill.
